------------------------------------------------------------
1. IDENTIFICATION STRATEGY
------------------------------------------------------------
• Method: Staggered-timing Difference-in-Differences (DiD) / Event-study estimated with individual and family fixed effects.  
• Idea: Compare changes in health-related behaviors of non-shocked relatives before vs. after an unexpected hospitalization of another family member (“health shock”) to changes over the same calendar time in relatives whose family has not (yet) experienced a shock.  
• Why appropriate?  
  – Hospitalizations for acute, non-elective conditions (e.g., heart attack, traffic accident) are plausibly exogenous to relatives’ prior health behavior.  
  – Population-wide, high-frequency administrative data give long pre- and post-periods and allow us to net out all time-invariant family heterogeneity and common macro trends.  
  – With staggered adoption (shocks occur at different dates for different families), the untreated families in each calendar month form a natural control group for families that are just experiencing a shock.

Mathematically (event-time specification):

Y_{fikt} = Σ_{τ≠-1} β_τ · D_{fk,τ} + γ_i + θ_{ft} + λ_t + ε_{fikt}

Y = outcome of relative i in family f, k indexes shocked member, t is month (or quarter).  
D_{fk,τ}=1 if relative i is τ periods away from the shock to family member k (τ=0 is month of shock, τ=-1 omitted).  
γ_i = individual fixed effect; θ_{ft} = family-by-calendar-year FE captures family-specific time shocks; λ_t = calendar time FE.

Event-time coefficients β_τ trace the causal response path.

------------------------------------------------------------
2. TREATMENT AND CONTROL
------------------------------------------------------------
Treatment:  
• A relative i is “treated” starting the first full month after another co-resident family member k experiences a first, unanticipated, non-elective hospitalization (index shock) between 1997–2011.  
• Key variation: exact calendar month of the shock.

Control groups / counterfactual:  
a) Within-person pre-period (DiD first difference).  
b) Contemporaneous relatives in families that have not yet had an index shock by month t (staggered DiD second difference).  
The identifying contrast is therefore (Post-vs-Pre for treated relatives) – (Post-vs-Pre for control relatives).

Sample construction rules  
• Keep only the first qualifying hospitalization per family to avoid multiple-treatment complications (later used in robustness).  
• Exclude elective hospitalizations and chronic-condition admissions flagged as “non-acute” in ICD codes.  
• Relatives: spouse/partner, biological/adopted children, biological/adopted parents, and co-resident siblings.

Outcomes
– # GP visits, # specialist visits, # filled prescriptions (by ATC group), preventive screenings, and longer-run hard outcomes (own hospitalizations, mortality).

------------------------------------------------------------
3. KEY IDENTIFYING ASSUMPTIONS
------------------------------------------------------------
A1. Parallel trends: In absence of a shock, relatives of families that happen to be shocked in month m would have followed the same outcome trend as relatives in yet-to-be-shocked (or never-shocked) families.  
   • Plausibility: Acute MI, strokes, or accidents occur unexpectedly; relatives cannot perfectly forecast the exact timing. Denmark’s universal health care limits financial anticipatory behavior.  

A2. No anticipation: Relatives do not change their health behavior in advance of the hospitalization.  
   • Plausibility: Sudden events give at most very short warning. Testable with event-study leads.

A3. Stable composition / no selective attrition: The set of relatives remains comparable pre/post; mortality of the shocked patient does not mechanically remove many observations of relatives.  
   • Plausibility: High.

A4. No spillovers to control families: One family’s shock does not immediately affect other, non-linked families.  
   • Plausibility: Social networks could spill over (e.g., close friends), but these effects should be second-order; we cluster SEs at family level.

A5. SUTVA within family holds up to the defined index shock (only one treatment per family).  
   • Addressed by first-shock restriction and censoring subsequent shocks in baseline spec.

------------------------------------------------------------
4. THREATS TO IDENTIFICATION & REMEDIES
------------------------------------------------------------
T1. Differential Pre-trends (violates A1).  
   – Remedy: Plot and formally test coefficients on leads τ=-6,…,-2 months; require they be jointly zero. Use family-specific linear trends as robustness.

T2. Confounding family-level shocks (divorce, job loss) coinciding with health shock.  
   – Remedy: Control for observable time-varying covariates (employment status, income, moves) of both patient and relative; add family-year FE; re-estimate excluding month of shock if it contains other events (registrations).

T3. Multiple / correlated shocks (patient’s condition may worsen, other relatives may be sick).  
   – Remedy: Baseline restrict to first hospitalization; alternative spec allows multiple shocks but uses cumulative event indicators; show robustness.

T4. Treatment effect heterogeneity and staggered DiD bias (Goodman-Bacon).  
   – Remedy: Use interaction-weighted estimator (Callaway-Sant’Anna) or Sun & Abraham (2020) method implemented in did or fixest packages.

------------------------------------------------------------
5. R CODE OUTLINE
------------------------------------------------------------
# Libraries ----
library(data.table)   # fast loading
library(fixest)       # high-dimensional FE
library(did)          # Callaway-Sant’Anna DiD
library(ggplot2)

# 1. Load data ----
dt <- fread("denmark_family_health.csv")   # one row per person-month

# 2. Variable construction ----
# Index hospitalization (non-elective) flag is already in data on patient rows
# Create first shock date at family level
setorder(dt, family_id, person_id, date)   # ensure sorted
dt[, shock_date := min(date[health_shock==1]), by = family_id]
dt[is.infinite(shock_date), shock_date := NA]

# Keep relatives (exclude the shocked patient itself for main analysis)
dt <- dt[person_id != patient_id_of_indexshock | is.na(patient_id_of_indexshock)]

# Event time (months relative to shock)
dt[, rel_month := as.integer((yearmon(date) - yearmon(shock_date))*12)]
dt[, treated := !is.na(shock_date) & date > shock_date]   # post indicator

# Winsorize event window to [-36, +60]
dt <- dt[rel_month >= -36 & rel_month <= 60]

# 3. Main regression ----
# Event-study with Sun & Abraham interactions
event_labs <- setdiff(sort(unique(dt$rel_month)), -1)  # -1 is omitted base
fml <- as.formula(paste0("gp_visits ~ i(rel_month, treated, ref = -1) | ",
                         "person_id + calendar_month"))
est <- feols(fml, data = dt, cluster = "family_id")

# 4. Robustness: Callaway-Sant’Anna aggregated ATT ----
cs_out <- att_gt(yname = "gp_visits",
                 tname = "month_id",
                 idname = "person_id",
                 gname = "shock_month",           # first treated period, NA for never
                 xformla = ~ age + gender,
                 data = dt)

agg_effect <- aggte(cs_out, type = "dynamic")  # dynamic ATT

# 5. Plot event-study coefficients ----
etable(est)
iplot(est, ci = TRUE)

------------------------------------------------------------
6. EXPECTED RESULTS
------------------------------------------------------------
Economic intuition suggests that a salient, acute health shock to a close relative raises health awareness and perceived risk, leading others to increase preventive and diagnostic care in the short run.

Prior expectation:  
• Immediate 6-month increase of roughly 0.1–0.2 GP visits per month (+8-15% relative to a baseline of 1.3 visits).  
• 5-year cumulative: 5–10% higher uptake of relevant prescription drugs (e.g., statins after a cardiac event).  
• Possible medium-run improvement in relatives’ own hospitalization rates for preventable conditions (small but negative effect, –2% over 5 years).

------------------------------------------------------------
7. VALIDITY CHECKLIST SELF-ASSESSMENT
(1 = clearly satisfied, 0.5 = partly, 0 = doubtful)
------------------------------------------------------------
1. Exogenous treatment timing (acute, non-elective)  ............. 0.8  
2. Parallel pre-trends (testable)  ............................... 0.7  
3. No anticipation  .............................................. 0.8  
4. No spillovers to control families  ............................ 0.7  
5. Correct inference for staggered timing (modern DiD estimator) . 1.0  
Average score .................................................... 0.80
